newsitem.title: USA: U.S. space shuttle heads for rendezvous with Mir.
newsitem.headline: U.S. space shuttle heads for rendezvous with Mir.

text.p: The space shuttle Atlantis rocketed off its Florida launch pad in a blaze of light and smoke on Thursday, on a mission to bring crucial supplies to Russia's Mir space station and swap a British astronaut for an American on board the orbiting outpost.

The $2 billion reusable spaceship carried a seven-member multi-national crew into a cloudless pre-dawn sky at 4:07 a.m. EDT (0807 GMT), beginning a chase through space after Mir which was scheduled to end when the two spacecraft dock at 10:34 p.m. EDT on Friday night (0234 GMT Saturday).

NASA officials said everything continued to go smoothly in the hours between takeoff and the astronaut's first wakeup call of the mission, just after 5 p.m. EDT (2100 GMT), to the music, "Those Magnificent Men in their Flying Machines."

"Good morning, and thanks for the magnificant music from the magnificent crew at Houston," Atlantis pilot Eileen Collins said after Houston mission control congratulated the crew again for the near flawless start to their 10-day trip.

During the next several hours, Atlantis's crew was scheduled to continue to refine the shuttle's path toward Mir, begin science experiments, monitor equipment and prepare for the docking and transfer of an oxygen generator and other crucial supplies to the ageing Russian space facility.

At about 5 p.m. EDT (2100 GMT), Atlantis was orbiting high above the east coast of South America while Mir floated over the Arabian Sea west of India, divided by about 6,866 nautical miles with Atlantis gaining steadily.
Atlantis was to pick up Jerry Linenger, of Eastpointe, Michigan, who has been working aboard Mir since January, and drop off his replacement, Michael Foale, a NASA astronaut from Cambridge, England.

The Mir space station was soaring high above the Indian Ocean west of Australia when the shuttle blasted off and its crew were unable to see the launch. Mir's Russian commander, Vasily Tsibliev, did however report seeing the shuttle's brightly lit launch pad through binoculars as the station later passed overhead.

"That's great," Linenger said after being informed of the successful launch. NASA administrators had joked about their desire to get the astronaut home in time for the expected birth of his second child in June.

The 42-year-old Navy captain and medical doctor will be relieved by Foale, who is to live and work on Mir until mid- September. Foale, who is married with two children, will be the fifth NASA astronaut to stay on the Russian station.
Foale was trained to help his cosmonaut crewmates maintain the 11-year-old space station, which has suffered numerous mechanical breakdowns, one of which led to a fire in February.
The shuttle's crew, which includes a woman pilot, a Russian woman, a Frenchman, natives of Britain and Peru and an astronaut of Chinese descent, is one of the most diverse selected by NASA.

Besides Foale, Russia's Kondakova, who spent 169 days aboard Mir in 1994 and 1995, and Collins, who became NASA's first woman shuttle pilot in February 1995, the crew included mission specialists Jean-Francois Clervoy, a French astronaut from European Space Agency; Edward Lu, an astrophysicist; Carlos Noriega, who was born in Lima, Peru, and Atlantis commander Charles Precourt.
Atlantis is carrying 4,000 lbs (1,800 kg) of supplies and equipment to Mir, including a replacement oxygen generator and repair gear to patch up a leaky cooling system.
